pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Brown Rot Blossom and Twig Blight Monilinia spp.

type_of_disease.quote: The fungi kill flowers, girdle and kill twigs, and cause maturing almond nuts and fruit to decay.

affected_parts.quote: Brown rot is a common disease in southern New England that affects blossoms, foliage, shoots, fruit and stems on susceptible trees.

summary.value: Blighted flower buds, brown and undersized foliage, wilted shoot tips, and scattered twig and small branch dieback; blossoms and the associated shoots wilt and die, and gum exudes at the base of infected flowers. Fruit infection first appears as small water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand to consume the entire fruit, and discolored decay spots develop on fruit and nuts.
summary.quote: Symptoms often include blighted flower buds, brown and undersized foliage, wilted shoot tips, and scattered twig and small branch dieback. Fruit can be infected at any time but susceptibility to infection increases as they approach maturity. Symptoms of fruit infection first appear as small, water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand to consume the entire fruit.

diagnostic_features.value: Cankers on blighted twigs have tan centers with dark margins, and during foggy, humid, or rainy weather gray to tan velvety spore masses form on diseased blossoms and twig cankers. Shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan (versus black for bacterial blast, which produces no visible spores). Diseased shriveled fruit may be held in the canopy as mummies, and stem cankers are accompanied by copious gum production (gummosis).
diagnostic_features.quote: Unlike the clumps or masses of gray and tan spores that develop on tissue diseased by brown rot when it is humid or wet, bacterial blast produces no visible spores. Shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan while those killed by bacterial blast generally turn black.

value: Bacterial blast, blight, and canker caused by the Pseudomonas syringae bacterium
Citrus brown rot caused by Phytophthora species
look_alikes.quote: Bacterial blast, blight, and canker caused by the Pseudomonas syringae bacterium produces similar blossom death, cankers, gumming, and shoot dieback on almonds and stone fruit. ... Citrus fruit that are almost mature can also develop a disease called brown rot . This malady is caused by Phytophthora species

value: Where available, choose plant varieties that are resistant to brown rot, and keep trees vigorous with appropriate cultural care.
Remove infected leaves, shoots and fruit to reduce inoculum within and around the tree; promptly remove and dispose of diseased shoots during dry weather.
Prune branches (and thin interior branches of young trees) during dry weather to maintain an open canopy for better air circulation and sunlight penetration, which promotes drying.
After working on an infected tree, clean tools and dip or spray them with a 10% bleach solution, 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, or a commercial disinfectant.
Use drip or furrow irrigation or low-angle sprinklers to avoid wetting blossoms, foliage, and fruit.
Avoid overfertilizing with nitrogen, and manage other diseases and pests that wound fruit or nuts.
Inspect green fruit at least weekly and remove affected fruit before spores form; cool fruit quickly after harvest and inspect during storage.
Chemical control is based on protection of flower parts; time applications to each cultivar's bloom stage, treating at pink bud (5-10% bloom) and full bloom.
One application at full bloom is sufficient in most orchards in most years with low rainfall; a second or third near full bloom may be needed in severe years or extended wet bloom.

Begin applications just before buds open (pink or white color) and repeat at regular intervals per label; e.g., myclobutanil or thiophanate-methyl at 20-40% bloom, with a second application at 80-100% bloom if high humidity or heavy rainfall follow.

Fungicides labeled for use against Monilinia include: calcium polysulfide, copper hydroxide, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, fenarimol, iprodione, mancozeb, propiconazole, sulfur, thiophanate-methyl and ziram.

Registered products for almond include pyraclostrobin/fluxapyroxad (Merivon), propiconazole (Bumper, Tilt), fenbuconazole (Indar 2F), difenoconazole/cyprodinil (Inspire Super), difenoconazole (Inspire), fluopyram/trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation), metconazole (Quash), fluopyram/tebuconazole (Luna Experience), azoxystrobin/propiconazole (Quilt Xcel), azoxystrobin/difenoconazole (Quadris Top), pyraclostrobin/boscalid (Pristine), iprodione (Rovral, Nevado) plus narrow range oil, pyrimethanil (Scala SC), thiophanate-methyl (Topsin M WSB), cyprodinil (Vangard WG), azoxystrobin (Abound), fenhexamid (Elevate 50 WDG), trifloxystrobin (Gem 500SC), myclobutanil (Laredo EW, Rally 40WSP), captan (various 50WP), and tebuconazole (Toledo, Tebucon).
treatments.quote: Remove infected leaves, shoots and fruit to reduce inoculum within and around the tree. Prune branches to maintain an open canopy for better air circulation and sunlight penetration... Begin applications just before buds open (when buds show a pink or white color). Fungicide applications should be made at regular intervals according to label recommendations. Fungicides labeled for use against Monilinia include: calcium polysulfide, copper hydroxide, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, fenarimol, iprodione, mancozeb, propiconazole, sulfur, thiophanate-methyl and ziram.

conflicts.note: UC IPM almond pest management guideline names the disease 'Brown Rot Blossom Blight'.

conflicts.canonical_value: Brown Rot Blossom and Twig Blight
conflicts.note: UMass extension names the disease 'Brown Rot of Stone Fruits'; all three records describe the same Monilinia brown rot complex and were merged.

UC IPM almond guideline attributes the disease primarily to Monilinia laxa, rarely M. fructicola. No NCBI/MycoBank taxonomy validation was supplied, so the genus-level umbrella name was retained as canonical.

conflicts.alternative_value: Monilinia fructicola, Monilinia fructigena, Monilinia laxa
conflicts.note: UMass lists three Monilinia species responsible for the greatest worldwide losses (M. fructicola, M. fructigena, M. laxa).

deltas.canonical_says: Shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan (versus black for bacterial blast, which produces no visible spores).
deltas.image_shows: Dead, shriveled flower buds show tan, dry blighted tissue with no galls, blisters, scabs, ooze, or fruiting bodies breaking through the bark.
deltas.image_quote: The affected area displays shriveled, dry, and tan-colored tissue indicative of fungal blighting.
deltas.reasoning: Tan, dry blighted flower/spur tissue matches documented brown-rot blossom blight, and the absence of galls/scabs/blisters is consistent with a Monilinia (not bacterial or gall-forming) lesion.

web_support.quote: Young blossom spurs and associated leaves collapse to form shoot blight; shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan, and cankers on blighted twigs have tan centers with dark margins.

deltas.canonical_says: Fruit infection first appears as small water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand to consume the entire fruit, and discolored decay spots develop on fruit and nuts.
deltas.image_shows: Dark, water-soaked streaks extend from a lesion edge, visible through translucent bark.
deltas.image_quote: There are dark, water-soaked streaks on the stem.
deltas.reasoning: Water-soaked lesion margins are a documented Monilinia sign, though the KB associates them mainly with fruit rather than stem bark, so support is partial.

web_support.quote: Infections begin as small light brown, water-soaked lesions that expand as the infection develops, and cankers on blighted twigs have tan centers with dark margins.
Small water-soaked lesions on the fruits gradually develop to soft rot covered with gray conidia.

deltas.canonical_says: Blossoms and the associated shoots wilt and die, and gum exudes at the base of infected flowers.
deltas.image_shows: Flower buds are wilted and decaying with significant necrosis, dominated by tan and chocolate-brown coloration.
deltas.image_quote: The affected tissue shows dominant colors of tan and chocolate-brown, indicating wilting and decay.
deltas.reasoning: Wilting and collapse of blossoms with brown-to-tan necrosis is the characteristic severity signature of brown rot blossom blight.

web_support.quote: Young blossom spurs and associated leaves collapse to form shoot blight; shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan.

deltas.canonical_says: Bacterial blast, blight, and canker caused by the Pseudomonas syringae bacterium; Citrus brown rot caused by Phytophthora species
deltas.image_shows: No stem pith color, petiole attachment, or other differentiating structural features are resolvable in the image to separate brown rot from its look-alikes.
deltas.image_quote: The photo shows a wilted blighted flower bud and leaves without clear stem pith, petiole, leg, or bract features.
deltas.reasoning: Coherent statement about image ambiguity rather than a positive symptom claim; published sources note the true brown-rot-vs-blast discriminators are spore masses and gumming (not pith/petiole/bract), so the observed absence of resolvable differentiating structures is plausible and uncontradicted but has no external corroboration, warranting curator review.

deltas.image_shows: The lesions are small and isolated, appearing as multiple holes along the margin.
deltas.image_quote: The lesions are small holes along the leaf margin.
deltas.reasoning: The 'holes in the leaf' morphology is the defining feature of shot hole, though the literature describes scattered blade lesions rather than a specifically marginal distribution.

web_support.quote: Spots on young leaves usually fall out, leaving a hole (the shot hole); older leaves retain their lesions.

deltas.image_shows: The lesion centers are tan, while the margins are chocolate-brown.
deltas.image_quote: The lesion areas show a tan center with a chocolate-brown margin.
deltas.reasoning: The tan center with a dark (purplish/brown) margin is the canonical shot hole lesion coloration reported by UC IPM.

web_support.quote: Leaf lesions begin as tiny reddish specks that enlarge by several millimeters into spots having tan centers and purplish margins.
Leaf infections are characterized by a lesion that is between 1/8"-1/4" (3-6 mm) in diameter, with a definitive yellow halo.

deltas.image_shows: The image displays necrotic tissue in discrete spots on the leaves.
deltas.image_quote: There are multiple holes around the margins of the leaves.
deltas.reasoning: Discrete necrotic leaf spots that later drop out are the core symptom of shot hole disease and are well documented.

web_support.quote: Leaf lesions... enlarge... into spots having tan centers and purplish margins... Spots on young leaves usually fall out, leaving a hole.

deltas.image_quote: The leaf is narrow and elongated with pointed tips.
deltas.reasoning: Almond (Prunus dulcis) foliage is botanically lanceolate, so the host leaf geometry is externally corroborated (though it is host botany, not a disease sign).

web_support.quote: The pale green leaves, up to 5 inches long, are simple, alternate, and lanceolate with serrated margins.

deltas.image_shows: The leaf has multiple holes along the margin, indicating significant damage.
deltas.image_quote: The leaf has numerous holes along its margins.
deltas.reasoning: Numerous coalescing shot holes are consistent with the heavy, defoliating infections shot hole is known to cause in California almonds.

web_support.quote: It is estimated that 80% of the California almond crop may be infested with shot hole disease, resulting in a potential yield loss of 50-75%.

deltas.image_shows: The leaves show curling up along their margins.
deltas.image_quote: The leaves are narrow and elongated with pointed tips.
deltas.reasoning: Extension descriptions of shot hole document discrete spots and shot holes but do not mention marginal leaf curling, so the observation is unsupported yet not directly contradicted.

deltas.image_shows: The leaf veins show various stages of damage, including clearings and necrosis.
deltas.image_quote: Leaf veins display both translucent areas and darker, dead sections.
deltas.reasoning: Published photo descriptions characterize shot hole as discrete round spots rather than vein clearing or vein necrosis, so no evidence corroborates this vein-based observation.

dropped_contradictory.image_shows: Multiple small holes on the leaf margins indicate marginal chlorosis.
dropped_contradictory.image_quote: The holes are located on the leaf margin.
dropped_contradictory.reasoning: Sources attribute the holes to excised necrotic lesion centers and the yellow/green halo (chlorosis) to a ring around each spot, so equating the holes themselves with marginal chlorosis misinterprets the described appearance.
